extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and beginning reporters (high school and college)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing effective news leads and organizing straight news stories (lead + body), aimed at teaching reporters how to summarize and develop news clearly and vividly. Emphasizes the inverted organization, the who/what/where/when/why/how test, active verbs, concision, and cautions/anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead is a summary of events (tell the climax first)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The lead is usually a summary of the events in the story... These [facts] he puts together as the lead. In other words, he tells the climax of the story first.", and the lead should then be developed step by step by supplying specific details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: gather all facts, view them as a whole, decide which facts give the gist, put them together as the lead (the climax first), then develop the lead in the body. If writing the lead first is difficult, the reporter may write the story in detail first and then write the summary, but the summary (lead) must appear at the top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead should answer the reader's who/what/where/when/why/how
rubrics_metrics.description: "Have I answered in my lead the questions that the curious reader would put to me to get the news in a nutshell—the who, the what, the where, the when, the why, the how of it?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every lead must answer all six questions, but an effective lead will answer most of them in order of their relative importance. General rule: a lead will tell who or what, where, when, and either why or how. Use this as a test when planning the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put the time element near the end of the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: "A good practice for high school journalists to follow is to put the when element near the end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing the time up front. Use the time element to close the lead rather than start or dominate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active verbs and concrete subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: "For this reason the main verb should be active and its subject concrete."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor active-voice constructions and concrete subjects to give the lead life and clarity. Example provided: a vivid active lead (Paul Kelliher dived... pulled an unconscious shipmate). Avoid passive or vague verb constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise and present main facts vividly
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads should present the main facts briefly and concretely (example: "In a lead of less than eight lines the main facts of the story are vividly presented.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a short, vivid opening (the book uses an example lead under eight lines). Develop other details in the body; keep the lead focused on the kernel of the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give full names the first time used
rubrics_metrics.description: "Give full names the first time used."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce people fully on first reference to avoid ambiguity; thereafter use last names or appropriate short forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't begin leads with weak/time/place openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Cautions: "Never begin a story this way: In the school auditorium, or At nine o'clock this morning, or Recently. The time element comes last in the lead."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns to avoid: opening with place/time phrases or vague adverbs like 'recently.' Start with the news action or significance rather than inert locative/time tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't begin with 'The', 'An', or 'A' unless unavoidable
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don’t begin with The, An, or A, unless there is no other possible way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stories that start with an article—seek more specific, active openings whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak, vague, or inflated modifiers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on bland intensifiers ('very', 'big'); prefer specific, concrete descriptors and active verbs to show significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple relative time words (yesterday, tomorrow) and clean date style
rubrics_metrics.description: "Say yesterday, tomorrow, last Friday, next Friday, rather than Friday, September 21. Say June 21, not on June 21st."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reader-friendly relative time words where appropriate; when using dates, use concise styling without superfluous prepositions or ordinal suffixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put the news into the lead — give the most important fact first
rubrics_metrics.description: "Put the News Into the Lead" and exercises that ask: Did the writer give the most important fact first? (The most important is the latest development.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads should foreground the most newsworthy or latest development. Inverted-pyramid logic: most important facts first, supporting details later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reporter presence in the copy (no we/our/I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise prompt: "Did the writer leave himself out of the picture (no we's, our's, I’s)?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News copy should be objective; avoid first-person references to the reporter or publication. Keep voice impersonal and reportive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subheads to break up copy and highlight high points
rubrics_metrics.description: "Insertions of this kind, called subheads, ... They suggest the high points of what follows."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place subheads to break up solid masses of copy, guide the reader to key points, and highlight the structure of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: News story structure: two parts — lead and body; develop lead with vivid details
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction and exercises repeatedly stress analyzing stories into two parts: the lead (summary) and the body (development). Exercises ask students to supply vivid details to make the body of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach reporters to identify what facts the lead sums up and what details belong in the body; the body should supply vivid, specific development and answer lingering questions left by the lead.
